tagline: Examination of the Irish milk metabolome for improved prediction of milk processability and sustainability.
funding: Funded by the Irish Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (project reference 2021R568).

studies.title: Pasture proportion in the diet
studies.summary: How the share of grazed pasture in the cow's diet and the season of the year shape the milk metabolome.

level_text.GRS: Cows graze primarily on pasture, relying on fresh grass as the main nutrient source. In this study the GRS diet was grazed perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne L.) through rotational grazing, about 95% of the annual diet, plus parlour concentrates (5%). The system is low-cost, environmentally sustainable and supports natural cow behaviour.
level_text.PMR: Combines grazing and a mixed ration. Cows grazed perennial ryegrass outside during daylight hours and were housed at night on the TMR diet at half the quantity. The PMR diet was 45% grazed grass (9 kg), 22% concentrates (4.5 kg), 22% maize silage (4.5 kg) and 11% grass silage (2.25 kg).
level_text.TMR: A fully controlled feeding strategy in which all components (silage, hay, grains, protein sources, vitamins and minerals) are mixed into a single ration. The TMR concentrates had 93.9% DM, with 22% CP, 23.9% NDF and 7.2% ash. The parlour concentrates fed to each herd (the sole concentrates for the GRS herd) had 89% DM, 13.3% CP and 30.9% fibre.

findings: The proportion of pasture in the cow diet had a significant effect on the milk metabolome.

Multivariate analysis (PLS-DA) separated the diets, with sample relationships changing in line with the proportion of pasture: GRS milks segregated clearly from TMR milks, while PMR milks resembled both.

Variable importance in projection (VIP) analysis highlighted 12 metabolites driving this separation: hippurate, propionate, succinate, valine, methanol, lactate, isobutyrate, formate, alanine, creatine phosphate, glucose-1-phosphate and dimethyl sulfone.
Hippurate was the most distinctive marker of diet, rising in proportion to the amount of pasture (AUC = 1.0 for GRS vs TMR).
studies.citation: Rojas-Gómez P, Pariyani R, Bateman LM, Lynch D, Timlin M, Dineen M, McCarthy NA, et al. Effect of proportion of pasture in the cow diet and seasonality on the milk metabolome as determined by 1H-NMR. Journal of Dairy Science 108(5): 4659–4673 (2025).
studies.design: 54 cows were assigned to three feeding systems (GRS, PMR and TMR) and their milk was sampled over 37 weeks (37 weeks × 3 diets = 111 samples). Skimmed milk was filtered through 3 kDa filters and analysed by ¹H-NMR, with spectral analysis and statistics in R and MetaboAnalyst 6.0.

studies.title: Seasonality of the pasture-based milk metabolome
studies.summary: The milk metabolome of Irish seasonal pasture-based dairy systems across the production year: 533 milk samples over 41 weeks.
findings: 30 of the 38 quantified metabolites varied significantly with season.

February (winter) milk, from early lactation, was enriched in ketone bodies, O-phosphocholine, creatinine and glucose-1-phosphate, reflecting metabolic stress and negative energy balance after calving.
Autumn milk, from late lactation, had more choline and urea, indicating better energy status but lower nitrogen use efficiency.

VIP analysis by season highlighted urea, N-acetylglucosamine, glutamate, choline, acetoacetate, creatinine, citrate, O-phosphocholine, glucose-1-phosphate, trimethylamine, fucose, hippurate and proline (VIP > 1).
Farm and shop milk profiles did not separate significantly (PLS-DA permutation test, n = 2,000, p = 0.087).
studies.citation: Rojas-Gómez P, Pariyani R, Dineen M, Lynch D, Bateman L, Roche E, Maguire AR, McCarthy NA, Murphy TB, O’Mahony JA, O’Callaghan TF. The MetaBó-Bainne Study: characterisation of the milk metabolome from a seasonal pasture-based dairy system using 1H-NMR spectroscopy. Food Chemistry (2026).
studies.intro: This study characterised the milk metabolome in Irish seasonal pasture-based dairy systems using ¹H-NMR spectroscopy. Seasonal, lactational and milk source-related variation was investigated across the production year using 533 milk samples collected over 41 weeks. The work sought metabolites and pathways associated with physiological adaptation, energy balance, metabolic stress and nitrogen use efficiency, and evaluated potential seasonal biomarkers.
studies.design: Over 41 weeks, raw bulk tank milk was collected weekly from ten dairy farms (n = 10 per week) and three commercial pasteurised skimmed milks were bought weekly (n = 3 per week): 13 samples × 41 weeks = 533 samples. Samples were defatted, filtered through 3 kDa filters and analysed by ¹H-NMR; 38 metabolites were quantified.
studies.season_def: Calendar seasons: Winter = February; Spring = March, April, May; Summer = June, July, August; Autumn = September, October, November.

design_figure.alt: Experimental outline of the seasonality study
design_figure.caption: Experimental outline: weekly collection of bulk tank raw milk and pasteurised shop milk, sample preparation (centrifugation, 3 kDa filtration, Chenomx internal standard), ¹H-NMR, spectral analysis and statistical analysis in R and MetaboAnalyst 6.0.

figures.title: Seasons (PLS-DA and VIP)
figures.caption: (A) PLS-DA biplot of milk metabolome profiles by season (component 1: 29.6%, component 2: 26.7%; R² = 0.255, Q² = 0.240, p < 0.001 from 2,000 permutations), with the metabolites contributing most shown as loading vectors. (B) VIP scores; metabolites with VIP > 1 are relevant for discrimination. The heatmap shows relative concentration in each season (red high, blue low).

figures.title: Months (PLS-DA and VIP)
figures.caption: (A) PLS-DA biplot of milk metabolome profiles by month (component 1: 32.1%, component 2: 24.3%; R² = 0.170, Q² = 0.158, p < 0.001 from 2,000 permutations). (B) VIP scores, with relative concentration in each month (red high, blue low).

figures.title: Farm vs shop milk
figures.caption: PLS-DA biplot of farm (bulk tank) and shop (pasteurised) milk profiles (component 1: 19.6%, component 2: 29.6%; R² = 0.377, Q² = 0.340). The permutation test (n = 2,000) gave p = 0.087, so the separation is not statistically significant.

items.caption: Mean concentration across months ± standard error (black line); each point is an individual milk sample.
